utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't mention this matter yesterday in court because I didn't want to cause any unnecessary embarrassment. The diskette was returned, and before I received a letter from Mr. Sayers by fax last night, Ms. Bower, who dealt with the diskette, had written to them on my instructions, setting out the position. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I turn to today's position before the Chamber announces any decisions it might otherwise have made about transcripts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've made no decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to be clear as to what the position is, and then we'll consider what we've got to rule on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that there is one or two points to be made clear. First of all, in relation to the Kordic Defence, if the Chamber would look at numbers 21 and 26, those are the two where Mr. Sayers and I, or one of us, are really to be attempting a negotiation. It was agreed. We have not yet been able to meet, simply for wont of time, to negotiate or discuss it. I think, frankly, we're going to have plenty of time this morning, I'm afraid, because I think we're going to run out of work to do, probably, and I would ask that they be put back so that we can consider them. I'm pretty optimistic that there will either be a compromise or it may be one or other of them can come to give evidence, but I hope that won't be necessary. I'm pretty sure we'll be able to reach a compromise on both. I hope so. Perhaps the next thing in order is what the Defence for Cerkez have by way of their position in relation to the various numbers they hadn't decided about last night. Again, for pressure of other things, I haven't been able to discuss it with Mr. Kovacic this morning, and I don't know if he's able to tell us anything now or if he wants to discuss it with me. I think he's got a little something to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may butt in unceremoniously, Mr. President, there are two witnesses whose closed-session transcripts had not been provided to us earlier, and I informed the Court that I would review them last night. With respect to Witness 17, subject to our overall objections regarding lack of confrontation rights and so forth, our objection to that witness would be withdrawn, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I follow the position on that. Are you withdrawing your objection or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We withdraw our specific objection. Our general position is that we disagree with the wholesale import of transcripts into the record, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But there's no particular objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No particular objection, that's correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And as far as 15 is concerned, subject to the last two pages being produced, again there is no particular objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No particular objection, and I must say I am almost certain that there will be no particular objection, even viewing the last two pages, if they are along the same lines as the materials that were provided to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my objections run along the same lines as Mr. Sayers's, and they are of principle nature.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in principle, they are the same and they still stand. However, I should, nevertheless, like to say, with regard to 12, because that is an important witness -- and my client believes that we do not have to expose that witness once again to that whole story about rape because that testimony is not particularly damaging, at least judging from the Blaskic testimony. There are still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. You're talking about 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Twenty-one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twenty-nine was a witness about whom the Kordic Defence had no objection. So that could be added to the list of those for whom there is no objection. While we're dealing with this, Mr. Kovacic, just so that we make sure everything is complete, number 48, would you look at that, please; the photographer to do with Zenica. Is there any objection, so far as you're concerned, about that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no 48. It goes up to 46. It must be some other number. I apologise. I'm sorry. I apologise. We had him but not on this list. We were given another list. No. No. We have no objections to that number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kovacic, is there anything else that you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I still have at least three who could be of interest for the decision in view of the opinion of the other Defence, but for various reasons, because we do not have the record or the absence of annexes or simply shortage of time, I'm still working on them. I believe that I could give you my definite reply about two of them on Monday, say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What numbers have you not yet completed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty-five, 32. We have a question about 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mine indicates that 32 had been removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So you needn't trouble about 32, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirty-four, 37, and 39. I do not think there is any need for me to go into detail right now. We do not have some parts of the transcript of the closed sessions. Some of them are lacking various attachments, annexes, and without them one cannot understand that, and some I simply had no time to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Nice, there is unresolved yet, and we have had no submissions, is number 47, General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And that raises perhaps another issue of rather general importance that I should have explored more carefully yesterday. My fault for not doing so. That means we may have to revisit one or two of our own applications. This relates to Defence witnesses generally. Can I explain, in straightforward terms, the problem? We've already done it for Blaskic, but I'll repeat it. Where a Defence witness gives evidence that can be separated into different topics, then of course some of those topics may be of importance and value to a case, and they may be wholly unchallenged. Examples are, indeed, the phone calls of which General Blaskic or Colonel Blaskic spoke, phone calls between him and Kordic, and particularly in view of the evidence about the tape, the other evidence about the tape of the transcript -- the tape and its transcript. We would like to have that part of the evidence in. There may be one or two other passages as well, but that part of the evidence in. We obviously don't wish to have the rest of the evidence in, which is exculpatory for Blaskic, who has, to a large degree, a common interest with this defendant, or with one of these defendants. Similar problems may arise in relation to other witnesses for whom we've already made applications. For example, a witness might give important evidence about the sighting of a piece of artillery, a factual piece of evidence, quite capable of being separated, out and we would want that evidence in while not necessarily wanting the balance of his evidence. Or a witness might give evidence of the involvement of Croatia, which could be separated out from his other evidence, which we might not want to go in as our evidence. So that the problem arises in relation to Defence witness transcripts in general: Is it appropriate to take simply part of their evidence when it can be properly compartmentalised in the way I've described? We would say there is no reason why not and every reason why that approach can be made. There's a particular reason why it can be made in this Tribunal, whereas it might be more difficult to envisage it happening in other domestic jurisdictions with which we're all and independently familiar. The reason why it can be regarded as appropriate in this Tribunal is that the general rule on taking evidence in chief is that cross-examination that follows is limited, subject to leave, to exactly that evidence. So if one imagines one of the witnesses for the Defence identified as witnesses whose transcripts we would like to be before you or whose transcripts in part we would like to be before you, if we envisage one of those witnesses coming to court and giving evidence on the narrow issue for which we would want them, then if that issue is non-contentious and if there was no question of further leave being given to cross-examine outside of that topic, then that would be an end of the matter. That is, of course, a practice particular to this Tribunal. So we would say, in general, that there is every reason -- and it's matter of practical good sense in the appropriate circumstances of a particular witness and case. It's practical, good sense to take evidence in part from Defence witnesses, particularly if they've been cross-examined if cross-examination on the topic was appropriate, and to let that evidence go in as part of the Prosecution's case. That will leave the position as follows: The Defence are always in a position to call that witness. Alternatively, at the end of Defence evidence, if evidence from that witness would be supportive of other evidence or is otherwise admissible as a transcript, then again part of it could be adduced to support their case. But our concern, my concern, and I have to say it relates not just to Blaskic but to two other witnesses with whom we dealt yesterday and, as it were, in respect of whom I might, as it were, be suspending our application at the moment pending resolution of the issue in principle, what we don't want -- indeed it wouldn't be helpful -- would be for one or more sentences from a witness, who was really adduced for transcript purposes for a particular topic by us but who said other things favourable to Blaskic and capable of being adopted by the Defence here, it wouldn't be helpful or desirable for those sentences to be counted as part of our case, because in an adversarial setting you've always got to recognise what may happen. You can't have it being said, "Here was a Prosecution witness who said this," when it's never part of the Prosecution's case. It's another reason for taking a realistic, if I may say so, view of taking transcripts from Defence witnesses in part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you move on, so that we know which witnesses you're dealing with, which of the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other two are the witnesses who we dealt with in private session yesterday afternoon, whose name we can't give but Mr. Scott dealt with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He wasn't numbered. He was simply additional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's not on this --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He's not on the list, but Mr. Scott dealt with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we don't have to consider him this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then the other -- the Court will remember that there was no Defence objection to his transcript, but if we can count that as the time being suspended, the Prosecution team generally, in any event, would like a little time in relation to these two witnesses. And the other one is number -- now I've lost the number, I'm afraid. It relates to the -- it's the artillery point that I was mentioning, and it's number 45. I'm sorry for not having been personally on top of this better yesterday -- I should have been, it's entirely my fault -- so that I could have invited you to deal with the argument in principle first before we then dealt with these three witnesses. You'll see the nature of the objection or the non-objection set out there, the Defence being quite clear about that. So I apologize to them for not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we will not consider 45 today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But considering Colonel Blaskic's evidence, what you would seek to do is to put in a part relating to the taped conversations?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct, or conversations generally, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Conversations generally. You would not seek to put in the rest, the other 5.000 pages or whatever it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely, and obviously we would have to, before -- maybe the matter can be considered in principle, and depending on the answer to that question, then we can be clear with the Defence exactly which pages we want to go in. And no doubt there would be room for discussion between us, because it would, of course, be right that if the Chamber took the view that any given topic was capable of being separated out and presented in transcript, then of course that topic, wherever it appears, in examination-in-chief or cross-examination, would have to go in. I accept that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's a broader question of principle with respect to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Just to remind you, Mr. Nice, about the new Rule 90, I think there is some answer to your question in "(H)", new "(H)" of Rule 90. In the cross-examination of a witness, and this is H(i), which is the former Rule, the cross-examination should be limited to the subject matter of the evidence in chief, which we know, and then we have the "(ii)". "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examination party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appeals which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." And then we have the "(iii)": "The Trial Chamber may, in the exercise of its discretion, permit inquiry into additional matter. " Now it is more open than you mentioned in your --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I quite understand that and accept that that's the drift of the Tribunal, although, of course, we are, for these purposes, I think, still working broadly on the earlier Rules. But that doesn't, I think, affect the principle. Nor, indeed, does it accept the general utility of this sort of evidence for the Chamber, because where you've got, say, a factual matter like the deployment of troops dealt with as a separate issue by a witness, not challenged in Blaskic, perhaps a military man likely to be independent and accurate on such factual matters, then it's likely to be helpful to have that evidence. But I'm grateful to Your Honour for reminding me of the change in the Rules. That's all I have to say on the general principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, speaking for Mr. Kordic and thinking on our feet here, let me make the following points with respect to the arguments that the Prosecution makes: As you correctly point out, there is a fundamental issue of principle which governs the determination of this matter. We would point out that there is nothing specifically in the Rules of Procedure and Rules of Evidence that permits the admission of transcripts anyway. It's a judicial decision that has resulted in that particular practice, the Aleksovski case. And we would submit that for the reasons I've previously articulated to the Court and won't go into again, that decision was not intended to open the floodgates of other cases' transcripts flowing into the particular case being tried where the particular defendant has no right to confront and certainly no right to cross-examine the witnesses whose transcripts come into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Remember what we said in Tulica, which is what we're likely to apply here, which is that it's for you to show what matters you would cross-examine on which haven't been covered in another case. But I accept that this witness is in a different category.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that he is in a different category, and I would suggest also to the Trial Chamber that there is nothing in the Aleksovski case, and I think there's nothing in the Tulica decision in this case either, that permits one party to pick over, as it were, the testimony of other witnesses, whether called by the Defence or called by the Prosecution in other cases, and to select out the bits and pieces of the testimony that they like while ignoring the bits and pieces that they don't like. We would submit that it's an all-or-nothing proposition. Either all of the testimony comes in or none of it comes in. That's a very simple position and that's exactly how it should be, and there's no reason for treating General Blaskic in a category that's different from any other witness, we would submit. I think that certainly this selecting bits and pieces of testimony raises most particularly the confrontation rights and the cross-examination rights that are embedded in the Statute and the Rules. Those rights are absolutely fundamental, and it's almost a slippery slope. Once you start chipping away at them, all of a sudden you've chipped away a lot before you've even realized that they are gone. They are precious rights and they can't be infringed. They are minimum guarantees. That's exactly what Article 21(4) of the Statute says. I'm sure I have no need to remind the Trial Chamber of that, other than to say that they are precious rights, and certainly from the perspective of Mr. Kordic, he regards those rights as precious too. And I think it's extremely dangerous when you adopt this eclectic approach, and we are opposed to it in principle. Furthermore, with respect to General Blaskic, and I don't want to overemphasise this point, but let me just remind the Trial Chamber that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can take it on a narrower point, can't you? Is there something that you would want to cross-examine about in Blaskic? Just thinking aloud about this, of course, what normally happens is that it was held that there was an identity of interest between, in Aleksovski, that case, the accused in that case and Mr. Blaskic, Colonel Blaskic. What is being sought to be done here is to put in a transcript of his evidence, the cross-examination being provided by the Prosecution, who cannot possibly be said to have had an identity of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's an excellent point and not one that I had considered particularly. But I think that -- now that I think about it, with respect to the particular points that the Prosecution would seek to adduce, even adopting the suggestion that the Prosecution has just outlined to you, it seems to me, anyway, that with respect to the subject matter of that testimony, there would absolutely have to be an identity of interest between the person that was subjected to direct and cross-examination and between the particular defendant in this case. We're speaking in somewhat theoretical terms. I fully realize that. It seems not to make a lot of sense to go much further, I suppose, except on matters of principle. But if the procedure that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, Mr. Sayers, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If the procedure that the Prosecution suggests were to be adopted, it seems to me, just thinking out loud, there would have to be an interest between the various parties just on those particular points, and I don't know what it is that they suggest, but I would very strongly suspect that there would be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Sayers slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to say, Mr. Sayers, on the Blaskic issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. With respect to the Tulica decision, we respectfully point out to the Trial Chamber that the two individuals involved in that decision were so-called village witnesses, I suppose, to use the vernacular that we've adopted in this trial. In that context, frankly speaking, it's hard to articulate a particular reason why a witness who has already testified and been subjected to the pressures that we've all seen this week should be dragged back to court to testify yet again to the same material. Insofar as village witnesses are concerned, it could be said, it seems to me, that there is a significant synonymity of interest between both defendants here and General Blaskic. But for witnesses who give testimony on other contested issues, more significant factual issues, it's hard to say there is a real synonymity of interest, and that's something that I just want to throw up for the Trial Chamber's consideration as it analyses these witnesses. I think that the village witnesses do fall into a different category different from the other significant factual witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the only point that I would add is that the Chamber is quite right to say there has been no cross-examination by a party with an identity of interest but the evidence has been led by a party with effectively an identity of interest, and that's the way I meet that point. But I have nothing else to add in amplification unless there is anything I can help you with in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will give our ruling in relation to the testimony of Colonel Blaskic. We are against the admission of that transcript for the reason which have been just recently adumbrated. First of all, we do not think it a satisfactory practice, unless there are particular reasons -- and there are none here -- why part of a transcript should be admitted. We think that if you're going to admit a transcript, normally you should admit the whole transcript. I would point out that is rather different, it is different from what we have invited the parties to do here, which is to point out what parts of a transcript they rely on. That is different to admitting only part of the transcript. There is a general point as to whether it is desirable or fair to introduce the evidence of an accused in one case against an accused in another, but we don't have to decide that, because we've decided on the grounds that we do not think selection is right in this case. Secondly, the decision which we have based our consideration on, namely, the Tulica decision which we gave in July, refers specifically to village witnesses who, as Mr. Sayers quite correctly has said, it may be wrong to bring back to give evidence about something in which the accused in this case, the two accused in this case, and Colonel Blaskic in his case, had a broad identity of interest. Now, in the case of Colonel Blaskic's own evidence, that cannot be said to be the case. There was no opportunity to cross-examine on behalf of this accused or anything like it. So we think that the application is misconceived, if one may say so, with respect, and we shall reject it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In those circumstances, can we count the other two Defence witnesses, that's Zeko and the one that Mr. Scott referred to yesterday, as suspended for the time being? We recognize that there are the two that I still have to discuss with Mr. Sayers; there are the three, I think, outstanding for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's take this item by item so we know what we have to decide on. Suspended on Prosecution application number --

Any ruling we make will be subject to any submissions by Mr. Kovacic in relation to those matters which he hasn't completed; that is, 25, 34, 37, and 39, and we'll hear anything he wants to say in addition on Monday, although we may make a provisional ruling in relation to those matters, subject to his submissions. There were some other matters which I thought that the parties were going to discuss; namely, 10 and 12, according to my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that there will be time this morning, because we'll clearly finish fairly early, for counsel to discuss what the best course to take about that witness is. Mr. Sayers, if would you also join in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may contribute -- sorry. If I may contribute to that slightly. Its a little bit difficult to talk about, but we have been informed during our investigation that this witness was practically expelled from the army of Bosnia after testifying in Blaskic. Not expelled but degradated a rank or so and sent in the place where God said good night. I mean, after that there were really problems. My client was in a good relationship with the person before the war, and we simply would not like to embarrass him once again. And our interest, which you mentioned, with our identity of the interests and cross-examination of Blaskic defence and our defence, I think there is really this particular situation there. There is no difference in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, if some agreement can be arrived at between counsel which means that he doesn't have to come to give evidence, so much the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm grateful to Mr. Kovacic for explaining to the Court the reasons why, no doubt, he's unwilling to come again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, it's also pointed out to me, and I see from my own note, that in regard to 38, there was to be some discussion about the excision of evidence. This is one of the BritBat witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right. This is the witness we require on a fairly narrow point, the village of Kazagici, but by your earlier ruling in relation to -- and the objection was, effectively, I think, that it was cumulative. By your general ruling in relation to Blaskic, I think the position might be that the witness's transcript could be admitted if you were so minded, but, of course, we would then, in accordance with our undertaking to His Honour Judge Bennouna in particular and all of you in general, we would then identify the pages that are actually material, which might be very limited in number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Can I just go through what we have so far to make sure we are all operating under the same rules and there are no mistakes. Suspended for Prosecution application, number 45; suspended for the parties to discuss, 21, 26, 10. I've got one other note which I cannot read. What was the other one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Twelve. That's Sefkija Dzidic, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twelve. Certainly. That must be it. Thank you. And you are calling Mr. Landry at number 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's certainly our intention, and he's agreed to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm operating on the understanding that the Prosecution are not now relying on nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thirteen and 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Twenty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thirty-two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thirty-three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And forty-two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Also correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, also correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that there is now agreement -- and if this is not the case would somebody point it out -- on 5, 6, 15, and 17, subject to the provision of some items of closed testimony which may change the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, as to 17, all of the closed testimony has been provided to us, and we withdraw our particular objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So 17, no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Fifteen is subject to the provision of two pages of closed testimony. Twenty-two, 29, and 48. Now, those matters being either agreed or not relied on, and some matters still outstanding, it seems sensible for us to consider the other matters. As I've said in relation to Mr. Cerkez, then any ruling we make in relation to matters which he has not yet completed will be only of a provisional nature in relation to what Mr. Kordic has said. But it would, I think, be helpful for us to make rulings on all these matters as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, and we would be very grateful for that, and indeed we would be grateful for the opportunity of having any subpoenas that we may seek consequent on the orders dealt with today if we are able to first decide and then get them in to a Judge in time. But it may not be possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we do adjourn, let me mention one matter concerning sittings next week. The Chamber have considered the position, and it would be convenient to one member or another to sit a shorter week, possibly three days in all. But it is subject, of course, to considerations of witnesses and the like. The proposal is that we should sit from 2.30 to 5.30 with a break on Monday, so not start until 2.30. We're not sitting Wednesday afternoon, and it would be convenient to one member of the Chamber not to sit on Wednesday morning. And of course we shall not sit, in any event, on Friday afternoon. Is that program going to present any problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that's not going to cause us any problems, and I'm pretty sure that the work we have to do next week can be accomplished within that time. If I find to my surprise that there are witnesses available in addition to the one very short witness I have for next week, I'll let you know, but I don't see it as very likely because methods of compulsion of witnesses and even methods of getting witnesses here by consent usually takes more than a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you've got one witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Only the one witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I thought there was an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, the one witness from Bosnia. Then there are the two investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two investigators, one in Bosnia, but there was talk of Mr. Landry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was talk of Mr. Landry. There's been no further information as to whether he's prepared to accelerate. I'm grateful to Your Honour for reminding me. I think he's still on the week of the 28th. He's coming from, I think, America.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So, effectively, there's about a day's work, though?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we've got the argument on dead and unwilling witnesses, and I must say something about that after the adjournment to make sure my learned friends are prepared to deal with one aspect of that. And indeed can I respectfully remind the Chamber that before I tell them about that, in theory, there is a decision to be made about one particular witness and his possible compulsion here and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That decision has been made and will be communicated shortly. It may be convenient if the parties consider what we should be doing next week rather than embarking on a lot of argument later this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've set out a timetable, I think, already, and my learned friends joining me want me to change some aspects of it because I hadn't adequately reflected their interests. But I think we can discuss the general timetable perhaps during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, we'll adjourn now. We'll consider this. We'll sit in half an hour, unless you get a message to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In giving our ruling in relation to the application for the admission of transcripts, I do so using the numbers of the various witnesses set out in the Prosecution motion for admission. I deal first of all with the matters which are not in dispute so that we have a complete record. No objection is taken now to numbers 5, 6, 15, subject to two pages of closed-session testimony which have to be provided, 16, 17, 22, 43, 29 and 48. These transcripts will be admitted, subject to the one matter I mentioned in relation to number 15, if there is a further submission. The Prosecution are not relying on numbers 9, 13, 14, 20, 32, 33 and 42. Accordingly, they will be excluded. The witness referred to at number 28 is to be called. The transcript will therefore be excluded. The Prosecution have suspended their application in relation to number 45, and they must notify us next week of whether they wish to proceed with that application or not. In relation to the following, consideration of the matters between counsel is continuing, and they will also be adjourned -- consideration on them will also be adjourned until next week. Ten, 12, 21, 26 and 38. Mr. Kovacic has notified us that he has not yet considered numbers 25, 34, 37 and 39, and the rulings which we now make are therefore subject to any submissions which he may think it right to make next week on those particular transcripts. I deal with the basis of our ruling, which is based on the decision which we gave in relation to what was called the "Tulica dossier" or binder of documents, when we fully considered what should be admitted, including transcripts, and it related to witnesses who had given evidence in the Blaskic case. We relied on the principle laid down by the Appeals Chamber decision of the 16th of February, 1999, in Aleksovski, with regard to the admission of transcripts, in which the Appeals Chamber noted that the disadvantage of a party not being able to cross-examine a witness whose transcript was admitted is tempered by the cross-examination in another case. In the Tulica decision, in which we considered transcripts of those who had given evidence in Blaskic, we ruled that they should be admitted, subject to any Defence application for cross-examination on the ground that significant relevant matter was not covered by the cross-examination in Blaskic. In the present case -- I should say that the Tulica decision was given on the 29th of July, 1999. In the present case, the transcripts also come from the Blaskic case, which is concerned about events in the same area, at the same time, with accused who were both -- all three, rather, Bosnian Croats. In one case, the case of Colonel Blaskic, he was a military leader, Mr. Cerkez also a military leader, and Mr. Kordic a political leader. Therefore, in relation to the background issues, that is, whether there was fighting in a particular instance, who started it, the nature of the fighting, the casualties, on those matters the same issues have been covered in both cases, and apart from the matters which we will deal with here during the course of this ruling, the Defence have generally not raised any significant relevant matter on which they say they are entitled to cross-examine or on which, in the view of the Trial Chamber, they are entitled to cross-examine in this case. Indeed, Mr. Sayers very properly pointed out this morning that to bring back witnesses to give evidence about these difficult matters for them is to put a burden upon them which, if possible, should be avoided. The first category of witnesses I deal with are very much under that heading, and that is what has been referred to as "village witnesses"; i.e., witnesses who come from the various towns and villages and give evidence of the background events which form the basis of these counts. The numbers which I deal with now are these: Witness numbers 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 11, 16, 23, 25, 34, 37, 39, 40, and 41. These are the witnesses about whom no concession is made. The complaints, as set out in the Defence document, are, in the view of the Trial Chamber, matters which goes to the weight of the evidence rather than whether we should admit the transcripts or not. So that includes references to hearsay, speculation by the witnesses, inconsistency in the evidence, and whether the evidence is relevant or not. All those are matters which the Trial Chamber would have to consider when deciding what weight to give to the evidence but does not provide a ground for excluding the evidence and certainly not a ground for saying the witness should be brought here to be cross-examined. However, there are occasions when exhibits are requested. They should be provided before the evidence is admitted. Likewise, any closed-session testimony. We would also note that the summary which the Prosecution have provided for us in their document is, of course, not evidence and merely an indication of what a witness says. Therefore, any objections to that are not strictly relevant. One witness is outstanding from this category, and that is number 36. We have considered this witness's evidence. We think that this is a witness who should be called, giving, as the witness does, direct evidence about one of the accused, and that's a matter upon which the accused would be entitled to confront the witness and cross-examine him or her. We turn next to the BritBat witnesses, if I may use that as a term or category. They're in a slightly different position to the village witnesses. Clearly, they have not had to live through traumatic events or nothing like as traumatic as the village witnesses, many of them. But nonetheless, the issue that we've considered in the case of these witnesses is whether their evidence really adds anything to the case which we have heard. Voluminous materials have been provided and are being provided, and we have to ask whether a witness adds anything or is just purely cumulative to the case as a whole. On that basis, I'm dealing with 18, 19, 27, 35, and 44. We will admit the evidence of numbers 18 and 44, because we've come to the conclusion that they may have new matter to deal with in relation to Ahmici and the events that day but not such as to call for additional cross-examination other than they have been subjected to in other cases, one in Blaskic, the other in Kupreskic. As for 19, 27, and 35, we think that different matters, different considerations apply. The Prosecution were not able to specify, with any detail, as to what additional matter these witnesses may be able to give evidence about, and we've come to the conclusion that they would be cumulative, and as such, they're not going to help us, and we will exclude their evidence. That, of course, would mean that we exclude their evidence as far as the transcript is concerned but also if there were any application to call them, which we would not encourage. Similar considerations may be said to apply to the two witnesses from the ECMM, number 30 and 31. Number 30 we will admit as having significant or may have some significant new evidence on this matter. Defence say about number 30 that there may be other matters upon which he could be cross-examined because of new documentation, but he was cross-examined in Blaskic and that, in our judgement, is sufficient and nothing new or significant has been mentioned. Number 31, on the other hand, we have come to the conclusion it adds nothing. We have had a considerable amount of evidence about these matters, which he covers. That leaves three outstanding witnesses who gave evidence in Blaskic, and as far as they were concerned, it's difficult to see how these accused and Colonel Blaskic could not have an identity of interest having regard to the matters about which they give evidence. In relation to number 3, Mr. Ashdown, the British politician who had conversation with Mr. Tudjman, we are satisfied that any matter for cross-examination would have been covered in Blaskic. The issue on the diary is not one which should lead us to exclude the transcript, although it may be -- on further consideration, we may decide not to rely on any evidence which arises from it, the Defence not having had the opportunity to see it. But as far as that goes, we shall have to look at the evidence in more detail before making a ruling. However, the transcript is admissible. Similar considerations apply in relation to number 46, again a witness giving evidence about conversations with Mr. Tudjman. He was fully cross-examined in the Blaskic case. The fact that there is no new material, the fact that there may have been further material which has been disclosed does not, in our judgement, amount to a significant matter for further cross-examination. In his case, diplomatic cables were quoted, which the Prosecution have not been able to obtain from the relevant country, the relevant state, but as we accept, the witness was fully cross-examined about that matter, about them during the course of his examination in the Blaskic trial and, accordingly, that the fact that they're not available does not prevent the evidence being given in this case. Again, it is not significant or relevant enough to cause exclusion. Finally, witness number 24 from UNESCO. We have come to the same conclusion about his evidence as we came to in relation to some of the BritBat evidence, namely, that there has been much evidence about the destruction of religious property, and in those circumstances, we do not see that this evidence is going to add anything to what we have already heard. And as far as the remainder of his evidence is concerned in relation to his opinions and the like, well, those are matters which, again, are not really going to assist us. We shall have to make our own minds up about those matters. For that reason, 24 is excluded, but 3 and 46 are admitted. I think that concludes the list of witnesses. If there's anything anybody wants to raise in due course, they can. Mr. Nice, could I ask the Prosecution, please, to provide these documents in coherent form, in binders with tabs and indexes, properly presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We could do that. Would it help if we identified the relevant pages, to assist, on that very document? We can most probably conveniently do it by marking the side of the page which a line, perhaps highlighting is a bit too extravagant an effect, but marking the side of the pages will we say are relevant. The Defence could have the document, perhaps before it comes to the Chamber, to mark in a different way the passage they would want you to rely upon, and in that way the Chamber's reading would be significantly reduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that can be done fairly rapidly, then yes. It would seem a sensible suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It does seem a sensible suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it would save what may be a long hearing, with us marking everything with highlighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll produce one, we'll provide it to the Defence for them to mark, and then we'll copy and distribute the double-marked document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If that could be done, again, as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I think that pretty well winds the position up for today. If I can -- it's a bit impertinent of me to say that. That concludes all I can deal with today. It's a matter of the Court, of course, when we come to an end, but can I just deal with a couple of things. As to next week's work, in addition to the material I identified or the topics I identified before, there's the possibility of two subpoena witnesses arriving. We'll have to wait and see. There is, of course, quite a lot of work being done, first between counsel and then possibly involving the Court, on the exhibit list. So I think one way or another, we may find that the available time will be fully used. I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: there is material going to show that he first denied, to some degree, and that may need clarification; secondly, made admissions about and, thirdly, made denials about certain events involving the defendant Cerkez. We will be arguing that all that material should now be before the Court for its consideration as part of that general argument on dead and unwilling witnesses. One other matter of detail. At the conclusion of Dr. Ribic's evidence, when he was being re-examined, some documents that had been gathered necessarily in haste for re-examination were put to him but not distributed. That exercise is going to be tidied up, as it must be, so that the documents are formally produced. We are, I have to say on this occasion, grateful for the fact that we aren't sitting on Monday morning, because it is going to enable us to do a number of things that we would otherwise have had to do either on Sunday or at some other time. The parties are going to be able to discuss the map on Monday morning, with a view to compromise or significant compromise. We will also be able to discuss the outstanding witnesses that the Court hasn't been able to deal with today on Monday morning, so all of those matters should be available for resolution on Monday afternoon or Tuesday. On Monday afternoon, there will be one very short witness, and I propose to follow that by -- if this is convenient to everyone -- the argument on dead and unwilling. Then on Tuesday, if this is acceptable to the Court, Mr. Elford can present his maps. I understand that we were due to be sitting in the small courtroom rather than this one. Two points on that. I think for the map exercise, the small courtroom will be very inconvenient, and speaking simply as counsel at this stage of the trial, when we are more likely to be here in larger rather than smaller numbers, this court is very much more convenient. However, although I can't say exactly what I know, I understand that there may be other difficulties with this court. Borrowing from what is said of mountains and Mohammeds, may I venture the suggestion that furniture is not immovable and it may be possible to construct this court in a way that is more comfortable for the Court than it may presently be, simply by using other furniture, because it is inconvenient, certainly for the map exercise, to use the small court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll make an inquiry about Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll be here on Monday and Tuesday, and then we can review the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that concludes all I have to raise today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness, anyway, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He made certain statements to the police in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then he made statements when he came to a democratic and free country, Australia. In those statements, he denied what he had said. They were disclosed to us by the Prosecution, but they were not entered into evidence. We thought that thereby the whole matter had been dealt with. However, yesterday my learned friend raised the matter, and we were given two statements, two witnesses, whom they appear they wish to use in connection with that unwilling witness whose name I shouldn't mention, and they are two witnesses who were first interviewed in January this year, that is, two or three weeks ago, who were never on any of the lists of potential witnesses. You made an order about that earlier on, about witnesses who had not been announced in advance. And a third point which I think is the most important one is that that is an attempt to introduce a statement given to the investigator as direct evidence in the case, and you have made a decision about that in your Tulica decision, where you said that those statements cannot be used as evidence. If the Prosecutor wishes to bring those witnesses, I think that according to the Rules, it is absolutely too late because the Defence will not be able to gather the necessary material to be able to cross-examine them properly. And another point that is very important, that this is multifold hearsay because they would apparently be telling us -- or at least one of them -- what this other potential witness may have said or actually said, a witness that we can't bring to court. I think that this is totally irrelevant, that even if all these witnesses were to be examined, the probative value of those statements or testimonies would be so limited that it is not simply worth the Trial Chamber's time to go into it. That is our position. If the Prosecutor goes on along those lines, of course, we will submit our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider these matters next week if they are raised. We'll adjourn now. Next Monday, half past two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
